svg.title: Coastal Forest — reconstructed poster
svg.desc: Reconstruction of the supplied Coastal Forest poster. The supplied forest PNG is embedded unchanged. Body text, headings and credit use the supplied Bookman BT Roman; the introduction uses the supplied Bookman Italic. The existing Bookman JF Pro swash title and slogan and the supplied outlined ministry logo are retained. The credit is separate right-aligned lettering in the black margin below the photograph. This is not a verified archival facsimile. The 24 by 36 inch page size is assumed.

g.aria-label: Coastal Forest

g.inkscape:label: 04 · Bookman BT Roman and Bookman Italic copy

g.aria-label: The mild climate, heavy rainfall and long, frost-free growing seasons of the
Pacific coast have created an environment that is unique in North America.
Almost six million hectares of lush coastal forest extend down the
western slopes of the Coast Mountains and across Vancouver Island and the
Queen Charlottes.
Exceptional Habitat
Exceptional Habitat
Exceptional Habitat, first column
It is the most productive commercial forest
in all of Canada, rich in stands of Douglas
fir, Sitka spruce, western hemlock and
western red cedar. But it also supports a
great number and variety of plants and
animals. Certain mammals such as the
Roosevelt elk and the coast deer have
evolved as unique subspecies. Band-tailed
Exceptional Habitat, second column
pigeons and bushtits are restricted to the
coastal area. Some plants, shrubs and trees,
such as the goldback fern, salal, Sitka
spruce and yellow cedar, grow in no other
part of Canada.
Areas of superabundant moisture have
created very dense stands of gigantic trees
that average 60 metres in height. Some
grow more than 90 metres, as tall as a 25-
storey building. In diameter, they measure
up to three metres. One would supply
enough wood to build several frame houses.
Early Exploitation
Early Exploitation
Early Exploitation
When Captain James Cook arrived in 1778,
he was overwhelmed by the number of
stands of giants like these. Concentrated
especially in the wet lowlands, they were
not only very valuable for lumber but readily
Exploitation followed. Early settlers
removed all the trees they could, either to
clear the land or to produce lumber. They
made no attempt to prevent soil erosion or
to leave seed trees to create new forests.
What logs they didn’t want to haul away
accumulated as fuel for later fires.
Hundreds of thousands of hectares of
mature coastal forest disappeared.
So did the land it was on—to forestry.
The fertile areas of the Fraser valley and
southeast Vancouver Island are now com-
pletely devoted to urban and agricultural
uses. They will never be forested again.
Integrated Management
Integrated Management
Integrated Management, first column
Today, samples of B.C.’s virgin rainforest are
preserved in parks such as Vancouver
Island’s Cathedral Grove. Some of the trees
predate Cook’s arrival by 600 years. But in a
province where half of every dollar depends
on wood products, we can’t keep loggers
out of the coastal forest. Instead, we are
working with them to establish logging
practices that do not threaten habitat for
wildlife and fish.
Cooperative planning determines the
least environmentally disruptive location
for logging roads. It also ensures that strips
of trees are left to prevent heavy erosion of
streambanks. Proper logging methods can
actually benefit wildlife such as deer and
blue grouse by opening the forest canopy
and encouraging the growth of fresh, young
forage. But animals like the Roosevelt elk
and some other species depend on mature
forests, especially during the crucial winter
season. Establishing reserves for them may
provide part of the answer, along with
Integrated Management, second column
designating areas where logging should be
deferred until the second-growth trees are
Whether or not such reserves or
deferrals are possible depends on our
own population pressures, and the recrea-
tional and industrial demands that we make
on our coastal forest.
